title: AI-complete
summary:
A problem is informally called AI-complete or AI-hard if it is believed that artificial general intelligence (AGI) would be needed to solve it, because the solution is beyond the capabilities of a purpose-specific algorithm. The concept is modeled after NP-completeness from computational complexity theory, where an NP-complete problem is believed to be as hard as the entire set of NP problems. By analogy, an AI-complete task necessitates the full suite of cognitive competencies that define human-level intelligence. The term was proposed by Fanya Montalvo in the 1980s.

A problem is considered AI-Complete if it can be solved by a Human Oracle and can be converted into any other AI problem via polynomial-time reductions. Examples of AI-complete problems include computer vision, natural language understanding, and dealing with unexpected circumstances while solving any real-world problem. Natural language understanding is often cited as an AI-complete problem because fully understanding human language requires not only parsing syntax but also interpreting context, humor, irony, and the speakers intentions.

Expert systems, popular in the 1980s, were able to solve very simple or restricted versions of AI-complete problems, but never in their full generality. When AI researchers attempted to scale up their systems to handle more complicated, real-world situations, the programs tended to become excessively brittle without commonsense knowledge. However, many of these tasks can now be performed by modern large language models.

The formal theory classifies AI problems into three categories: AI-Complete (problems solvable by Human Oracles), AI-Hard (problems that resist such solutions and are considered at least as difficult as any AI-Complete problem), and AI-Easy (problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine with an oracle for some AI problem).
